gap: No result ChatGPT got explains that the 'Power Lifting', 'X-Boost' and 'Lifting Power' numbers makers print next to continuous output (2,200–2,700 W on the 1 kWh units) work by lowering the output voltage, so a heater running on them gets less power and gives less heat; and BLUETTI sells a 600 W station with a printed '1,500W Lifting Power' that looks like it matches a 1,500 W heater but does not.
standout_why: I opened testedwatts.com, voltandvalley.com, lightsonlab.com and utrendco.com (all four cited) on 2026-11-14. All four say the heater must fit under the continuous rating. Only Volt & Valley mentions X-Boost or SurgePad, and only as one number each (DELTA 2 Max '3,400W available through X-Boost', C300 '600W SurgePad'). None says these modes lower the voltage, none says a heater gets less heat on them, and none gives a lifting figure for any 1 kWh unit. None notices that EcoFlow's own store gives two different X-Boost figures for the 1,024 Wh DELTA 3 line (2,200 W and 2,600 W). Our current page has an 'AC continuous' column but no lifting column and no footnote about this.
decides: This backs the current pick: the 1,800–2,000 W continuous units (AC180, Elite 100 V2, DELTA 3, C1000 Gen 2) run a 1,500 W heater at full power without using any lifting mode. A unit that only reaches 1,500 W through Lifting, X-Boost or surge (for example the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2: 600 W rated, '1,500W Lifting Power') would run the heater at lowered voltage and noticeably less heat, so it is out. The Jackery 1000 v2 is rated exactly 1,500 W, and I found no lifting mode on its page, so it has no margin. The page should keep it marked 'at its limit'.

Both units are 1,024 Wh / 1,800 W, but EcoFlow's US store prints 2,200 W X-Boost for one and 2,600 W for the other. The continuous figure (1,800 W) is the one that is consistent across both.

findings.label: How X-Boost works, in the maker's words
findings.value: 'intelligent voltage control that marginally reduces voltage, allowing you to power devices with a lower-rated inverter'; it lists 'Electric Heater: 2200W' as an example load
findings.note: This is EcoFlow's South African page; the US page did not load. The wording is quoted from that page. Arithmetic (mine): a resistive heater's power goes with voltage squared (P = V²/R). A 1,500 W @ 120 V heater held to 1,000 W would need about 98 V (120 × √(1000/1500)), and would give about a third less heat. That is why X-Boost or lifting is not a substitute for continuous watts with a heater.

findings.note: Store search via storecheck. The current SG 1000 v2 text says '1024Wh Capacity and 1500W Output'. The refurbished Explorer 1000 v2 listing (https://www.jackery.com/products/jackery-explorer-1000-v2-portable-power-station-refurbished) says '1070Wh Capacity and 1500W Output'. Our page lists 1,070 Wh, so this needs checking. Neither listing mentions a lifting or boost mode. With 1,500 W continuous against a 1,500 W heater there is 0 W of margin.
